moments.title: She asked the man who manages her assets for the full history, the same morning
moments.summary: Asked how confident she feels after the course, a participant says she has already acted on it: that morning she asked the person who manages her assets for the whole trajectory since she began, because she now wants to see what has been done, understand it, make changes, and diversify. She says she never thought about it in all this time.
moments.evidence: I asked my guy who manages my assets and we are full trajectory from the day I began. Actually I want to see what I have been doing. I want to understand also and then make changes and I am actually thinking of diversifying and investing differently.

moments.title: She was afraid of investing; the shift was realising it is not that tough
moments.summary: A second participant says she was really afraid of investing and never wanted to learn anything about it, and that the big change is simply understanding — she repeats "I understand" three times and lands on "it is not that tough".
moments.evidence: I was really afraid of, like investing never wanted to learn anything but yeah this is really made it. I mean I feel like I can understand. I think big learning for me has been like oh I understand, I understand, I understand. It is not that tough.

moments.title: The aha moment: how an SIP compounds, and that she can still start for her kids
moments.summary: Asked for the biggest aha moment, the answer is compounding — she felt she had missed the bus, then realised she can start for her children instead, and says it is crazy how it compounds and that she never realised it was like that. The transcript renders compounding as "bounding of the SIP".
moments.evidence: bounding of the SIP. Yeah. And you know it was just wow. Like the longer you called it I just felt like I missed the bus. But no for our kids we can start, it's just crazy how it compounds.

moments.title: Judging a fund against the index instead of in absolute terms
moments.summary: A participant says the useful shift was in how to evaluate: people look at returns in quite absolute terms, and benchmarking properly against the index gives a deeper view of what is working and what is not.
moments.evidence: we look at it in quite absolute terms but I think when you're benchmarking in the right way against the index it gives you a slightly deeper perspective

moments.title: Family money felt like it was in "more able hands", so she never stepped in
moments.summary: Asked what she has since said to her husband or father, a participant describes the default she is leaving behind: when family money is already being managed you assume those are more able hands and so you do not get involved at all. What has changed is wanting to treat it as a unit, be aware, and be part of the conversation.
moments.evidence: when typically money you have as a family is being managed. You feel like those are more able hands so then you don't really step in or get involved at all. But I think it is important to look at it still as a unit and be aware and part of the conversation
